title: Alabama Power v. Fenn Church headed to Supreme Court - WBMA
content: What legal argument is Alabama Power using to appeal the injunction? What is the total cost and length of Alabama Power's transmission line project? Why was a preliminary injunction granted against Alabama Power's property access? SHELBY COUNTY, Ala. (WBMA) — The legal battle between Alabama Power and Fenn Church over a Shelby County property is headed to the Alabama Supreme Court. Alabama Power is appealing a circuit court order that prevents the company from entering Church's property while the condemnation case is being appealed. In its latest court filing, Alabama Power argues the circuit court erred by blocking access to property the company says it has a legal right to enter under Alabama's condemnation laws. The company also argues the Church defendants have an adequate remedy through monetary compensation and that Alabama Power has already paid the condemnation award into court and posted a bond. The dispute involves a 74-mile, $248 million transmission line Alabama Power says is needed to relieve overloading on its existing electric grid. The company says the section crossing Church's property represents about 0.55 miles of the project. A preliminary injunction was granted after a two-day hearing. The court considered concerns involving Church's home, privacy and safety, as well as Buxahatchee Creek and old-growth trees. Alabama Power has said it needs access to the property to keep the project on schedule for a May 2027 completion.

title: Petersburg High School cross country girls win Region V Championship in Juneau - KFSK
content: Every girl and one boy on Petersburg’s high school cross country team are heading to the state championship in Anchorage this weekend. That’s after strong performances at the Region V Championship in Juneau last weekend. Head Coach Kayleigh Lenhard said the team did well across the board. “I think every single one of our runners had either a personal best or probably a season best for their cross country runs this season, which is pretty hard to do on the Juneau course,” she said. “So I think everyone was pretty happy with their performances.” The Petersburg girls team took first place in Division III, and every Petersburg girl placed in the top 12. Junior Arielle Tucker placed second with a time of 20:53.2, junior Cadence Flint placed third with a time of 21:44.4, and freshman Arya Holmgrain took sixth with a time of 22:30.3. The boys ranked fourth overall. Sophomore Andi Mihai placed third with a time of 18:11.8, earning him a state spot. “Everyone was really excited, really proud, and Andi was probably the most surprised because he was ranked sixth, and so he wasn’t expecting to get third place,” Lenhard said. “But he just had a really good day out there, and so I was really happy for him.” Now the team has turned their eyes to the state championship on Saturday, October 3. Lenhard said they’ve been focusing on combating nerves. “The girls really want to win, and we are right now kind of ranked to win, but like I said before, you never really know what can happen,” she said. “So we’re gonna keep on working hard this week and go in and give it our all, just like they always do.” Lenhard said the team is working to maintain existing routines, eat well, and get good rest ahead of state.                     Steve Douglas, Associated Press It's a years-long controversy that has gripped English soccer and beyond: Did Manchester City's ownership engage in large-scale rule-breaking in an effort to transform the team into a global superpower and serial title winner? In a stunning verdict announced Tuesday, the Premier League published a statement confirming City was guilty of almost all of the 115 charges leveled against the Abu Dhabi-controlled club for alleged breaches of financial rules in the world's most popular league for much of the last two decades. READ MORE: Manchester City captures Premier League title "This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history," said Richard Masters, the league's chief executive. There are likely to be seismic ramifications when sanctions are eventually handed out to City, with a whole range of punishments on the table — including expulsion from the Premier League. And what will happen to City's squad of superstars that includes Norway striker Erling Haaland and Argentina midfielder Enzo Fernandez, signed this month for $169 million? Here's a closer look at the case that everyone in soccer is talking about: In February 2023, the Premier League went to battle against its own champion team in unprecedented fashion, releasing a long statement detailing a list of 80 alleged breaches of its financial rules by City from 2009-18, the first nine seasons under Abu Dhabi ownership as the club tried to escape the shadow of great rival Manchester United. The violations included failing to provide accurate financial information and submitting inflated figures for sponsorship deals out of Abu Dhabi; hiding payments that supplemented salaries of managers and players; and breaching financial rules established by the Premier League and UEFA, European soccer's governing body, aiming to keep clubs financially stable by not spending beyond their means. The league also accused City of 35 more breaches relating to its alleged failure to cooperate with the investigation from December 2018. The charges stemmed from purported internal emails from City published by German outlet Der Spiegel which, it claimed, detailed schemes by the club to allegedly cover up true sources of income in a bid to comply with financial fair play regulations. The information published by Der Spiegel was unearthed by the "Football Leaks" website, whose founder is Rui Pinto — a Portuguese computer hacker. The announcement the soccer world was waiting for came Tuesday — and it was explosive. City was guilty of all the financial breaches in the 2009-18 period and the majority of the charges of non-cooperation, the league said. Standing out in the findings was the revelation that City arranged what the league described as "sham" contracts with commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than 830 million pounds ($1.1 billion) by the Abu Dhabi ownership. The commission also said that some witnesses called by City to the hearing gave evidence "they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest." "By its conduct the club clearly intended to circumvent" Premier League rules, the commission added. The club did not dispute the authenticity of any initial published emails but said they were "out-of-context materials purportedly hacked or stolen from City Football Group" and that it was an "organized and clear" attempt to damage City's reputation. When the Premier League announced its charges in 2023, City said it was "surprised" by the allegations and that it welcomed an investigation by an independent commission "to impartially consider the comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that exists in support of its position." City chief executive Ferran Soriano again referenced that "irrefutable evidence" in an internal video to club staff — obtained by broadcaster Sky News — that detailed why he felt the verdict was wrong. Soriano said the Premier League's case against City was "based on a single false accusation: that the owner's personal money was somehow and secretly put into the club via some sponsors from Abu Dhabi. This is just not true." In a separate statement issued by the club, City called the commission's findings an "opinion" that "contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe." City would be appealing against the verdict and will be "relentless" in attempting to clear its name," the statement said. The Premier League said sanctions will be decided in a separate, confidential hearing held by the same independent commission at an unspecified date. It also depends on the completion of the appeal that City needs to lodge by Friday. According to Rule W64 of the Premier League handbook, there is a range of sanctions available to the commission, from a fine, to a points deduction to expulsion from the league. For context, Everton was given a record 10-point deduction in 2023 — later reduced to six — for overspending in one financial period (three years up to the end of the 2021-22 season). City's charges are much, much wider — and unlike Everton, include a refusal to cooperate. An appeal by City will lead to a three-person Appeal Panel being set up. Sky Sports has reported that City could go to the High Court in London if it feels the process in the case was unfair and/or impartial. UEFA previously accused City of overstating sponsorship revenue to comply with Financial Fair Play regulations, based on the same documents published by Der Spiegel. In 2020, UEFA ruled the club had committed "serious breaches" of those regulations from 2012-16 in handing out a two-year ban from its competitions. That ban was overturned by the Court of Arbitration for Sport, which said some of UEFA's allegations were not proven and others were "time-barred." CAS, instead, imposed a 10 million euro ($11.3 million) fine on City for failing to cooperate with independent investigators. There are already reports that rival clubs have been preparing compensation claims on the basis that they have been impacted by City's rule-breaking. A precedent was set just this year, with Everton ordered to pay more than 35 million pounds ($47 million) in compensation to Burnley, which successfully argued to a disciplinary commission that it would have survived relegation at Everton's expense in the 2021-22 campaign had its rival been given its six-point penalty for the financial breaches that season. It's unclear if City could be stripped of its Premier League titles, though a line in the competition's handbook — that the commission can "make such other order as it thinks fit" — leaves such an option on the table, in theory. Relegation from the Premier League would surely lead to the breakup of its squad of superstars. Away from the field, a finding of systematic rule-breaking is a major blow to the reputation of Abu Dhabi, whose purchase of a top soccer club in England has been described by some commentators as a soft-power strategy at a time when other Gulf states have invested heavily in the sport. "I said to them, if you lie to me, the day after I'm not here," then-City manager Pep Guardiola — the coaching mastermind behind most of City's title wins — said in 2023. "I will be out and you will not be my friend anymore." Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Left:

title: The 2027 Hyundai Tucson Is Ready To Give RAV4 And CR-V A Real Fight - CarBuzz
content: Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update When the time comes for a car company to redesign its bestseller, it's understandable if the result is pretty similar to what was already available. That's the path Toyota took when updating the RAV4, which topped both Toyota's and America's sales charts, excluding a certain pickup truck line. Toyota gave it freshened styling, and made it hybrid-only, and that was about it. Hyundai, on the other hand, is going in a very different direction. The 2027 Tucson might as well be a different model than its predecessor, even if it has some rough size and powertrain similarities. While the previous Tucson had its fair share of sharp creases and planes, the overall shape was still rather sleek and curvy. The hood had a gentle slope to it, and the roofline seemed to arc from front to back. It also had a prominent, geometric grille into which the running lights blended. All of that is out the window with the new Tucson. The hood is nearly horizontal, and as Senior Vice President and Head of Hyundai Design Center Simon Loasby noted, the hood also extends right over the tops of the fenders to emphasize the SUV's width. The nose is mostly blunt and solid, and it's bracketed by a pair of vertical running lights and a horizontal light bar. It's futuristic and a bit imposing, like something that could've come out of Omni Consumer Products. The angularity of the Tucson is more evident in profile. The roofline is a straight edge that's angled slightly down to the rear. Crisp lines accentuate the blister fenders, which are further pumped up by trapezoidal black plastic fender flares. Hyundai has managed to keep it from looking too slab-sided, simplistic, and stocky, though, with the addition of contrasting silver trim along the rockers and the bumpers. Surprisingly, the most impressive bit of design on the Tucson is at the back. The taillights are sort of a mirror image of the front running lights, but the taillights are transparent, crystal-like structures that wouldn't look out of place on a current Cadillac EV. The light bar across the tail uses indirect lighting, a bit like that on the Tesla Model Y, so the light you see is actually reflected off the tailgate. The tailgate itself has other neat details, particularly the way the edges of the rear window sill rise to meet the line from the side, and the intricate folds at the tailgate's bottom edge. Besides the fresh styling, the Tucson is larger, too. It's 2.4 inches longer, 1.6 inches wider, and 0.8 inch taller. In comparison to the class benchmark, the Toyota RAV4, the Hyundai is 4 in. longer, 2 in. wider, and about even for height (actually 0.2 in. shorter). The bigger, wider, bolder body is also wrapped around a new unibody platform that Hyundai says is even stiffer than before thanks to additional high-strength steel and welds. Hyundai is also introducing a new XRT Pro trim, and it has its own set of cool details. It has unique front and rear bumpers, with the front one rising higher with larger grille openings. Naturally, it has big red recovery hooks, which are square in shape to keep with the design theme. It also loses the silver trim along the sides in favor of extra matte black cladding. The fender flares and cladding both feature a molded-in pattern inspired by forged carbon fiber, and is similar to what Hyundai uses on the Ioniq 5 XRT. It has unique 17-in. wheels with all-terrain tires, and the rear bumpers are chunkier, too. Up on top are a pair of roof rails with a nifty detail in its forward-leaning edges above the front doors. The XRT looks even a bit more imposing, and gains some off-road capability, thanks to a 1.2-in. lift, bringing ground clearance to 8.3 in. The Tucson's cabin is just as much of a radical departure from the previous generation as the exterior. It's also not what you would expect. Instead of hard edges, nearly every surface is curved and rounded. The dash panels even look like they're cushioned, almost like a Chesterfield sofa. It's all meant to make the interior as comfy and relaxed, almost like a "living room" as Loasby put it. To that end, there's indirect ambient lighting, and the driver's right armrest extends almost to the center stack. Hyundai also gave the Tucson an overhaul when it comes to instruments and infotainment. The wide double-screen monolith that's become so common is gone. Now, the driver gets a thin 9.9-in. display showing only the most important information such as speed. The center screen is quite large, measuring 12.9 in. on the base models, with a huge 17-in. unit available. It runs Hyundai's latest Android Automotive-based operating system, with an AI voice assistant available. The screen also houses some key indicator and warning lights that would have previously gone into the instrument display. Right below the center screen is, to our great relief, physical toggles and buttons for climate and audio controls. The XRT Pro also gets a few unique interior features. The dash panels are made up of black and dark metallic plastics, and the seats are an earthy tan. The seatbacks also get some extra detailing in the form of a de-bossed mountain range design. Finally, because the Tucson is bigger on the outside, it's also bigger on the inside. Most of the expansion is for the rear seats where in addition to more head and shoulder room, Hyundai claims to have added more legroom. It's easier to get back there, too, thanks to rear doors that open to 83 degrees, rather than 73 on the old version. Cargo space also grew from an SAE-rated 38.7 cubic feet behind the rear seats, to 41.7. Under the broad hood of the Tucson lurks one of two engine options, and they're a bit different than before. The outgoing Tucson featured a naturally-aspirated 2.5-liter four-cylinder. That's gone, replaced by a turbocharged 1.6-liter four-cylinder. The amount of horsepower remains the same at 187, but torque is up by 17 pound-feet to 195. It's still paired with an eight-speed automatic and either front- or all-wheel drive. Hyundai estimates it to get to 62 mph in 9.5 seconds. Fuel economy will range between 26 mpg combined for the all-wheel-drive version, and 28 mpg for the front-drive one, and those are identical to the 2.5-liter engine. The Tucson naturally still gets a hybrid powertrain as an option, and the numbers are almost identical to before, though the powertrain has been updated. The turbo 1.6-liter four-cylinder and its electric motors weigh a bit less than before thanks to fewer parts and some small changes like the use of an electric water pump. The hybrid is also more efficient, with economy ranging between 38 mpg combined at the low end, to 42 at the high end, tying some of the more efficient RAV4 variants. The previous version ranged between 36 and 38. Power is basically unchanged at 232 hp combined, and torque is up slightly from 271 lb-ft to 280. The extra power compared to the non-hybrid. The hybrid also gets a nifty new feature called HEV Stay Mode. It allows an occupant to shut off the car, but keep the climate control running entirely off the hybrid battery, so that you don't have to use fuel to stay cool or warm while waiting in the car. It does have a limit, with power lasting about 30 to 40 minutes before you would need to fire up the engine again. Interestingly, the XRT Pro model is only available with the hybrid engine. Hyundai's Senior Vice President for Product Planning and Mobility Strategy Olabisi Boyle said the reason was mainly for the increased performance. Of course, the efficiency was surely appealing, too, along with the fact that the trim should be a high-level one that would accommodate the cost of a hybrid powertrain nicely. Hyundai also added a couple of other trail assists to go with the improved ground clearance and approach, departure, and breakover angles. In addition to the manually selectable snow, mud, sand, and rock drive modes, the XRT Pro gets something called Smart Terrain Assist. It automatically switches between those off-road modes while determining the type of terrain and informing the driver of the difficulty of said terrain via the instrument display. It has a low-speed cruise control, too, similar to what many Jeeps have. It won't crawl the vehicle over rocks like a Toyota or Ford, but it provides finer speed control on trails. There is one powertrain missing from the American lineup for this new Tucson, though. The plug-in hybrid has been dropped, though it will continue to be available in other markets. Boyle said that low demand was a major reason for dropping it. All the remaining Tucson powertrains and their respective models will go on sale in the first quarter of next year, and we should get pricing sometime closer to launch. As we've mentioned, the Tucson is Hyundai's top seller, so it's critical that the company gets it right. Going in such a dramatic new direction, styling-wise, is a bold choice, but we think the company is on the right track. Buyers are still showing a preference for tougher, boxier, and more off-road-oriented vehicles, and the new Tucson leans into those ideas. Plus, it's more spacious, and the hybrid is even more efficient than before. With all these factors combined, the Tucson should be a huge success for Hyundai, and should have Toyota and Honda nervous. We want to hear from you. title: Ireland v Austria: Are match tickets on sale? Will there be protests? Where can I watch on TV? - The Irish Times
content: The Republic of Ireland will play Austria in their third game of the Nations League in League B, Group 3. The game kicks off at 7.45pm on Thursday at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin. You can watch the game on RTÉ2, coverage is back to normal after the stripped down broadcast from the Israel match, beginning at 7pm. In the UK, you can watch the game on Amazon Prime PPV. The main question is if Gavin Bazunu joins the team for the match against Austria after the goalkeeper withdrew from the Israel game, saying “it would be wrong to participate”. Manager Heimir Hallgrímsson said the plan is that he will be with the squad against Austria, but not against Israel in the second game. Otherwise there were no significant injuries reported from the Israel match. Liam Kitching made a case to start after an impressive debut against Israel, as did Jack Moylan with a fine goal and assist in Hungary. Finn Azaz, a regular starter, was left on the bench against Israel and it is not clear if he will return to the starting line-up. Hallgrímsson said of his decision to leave him out Azaz: “We thought he wasn’t ready to play. He wanted to play, but it was my decision. He wasn’t fit enough to play this game.” On Thursday morning the FAI announced that the match is sold out with no more tickets available. It is also worth noting for those attending the match that the Lansdowne Road Dart Station will close temporarily on Thursday from 3.30pm until end of service, with supporters advised to get off at Grand Canal Dock or Sandymount stations. The FAI have moved hundreds of fans with pitchside seats for the game amid concerns the game will be interrupted by protests. The FAI says the decision was made because the Austria match is being used as a test event for the staging of Euro 2028 games, but FAI sources also admit that the seat moves will help act as a buffer against any potential pitch invasions. Ireland’s most recent home game against Qatar in May was interrupted by several tennis ball protests by advocates for a boycott of the Israel games. “I would see [the Austria game] being a serious question mark from an industrial point of view regarding transport, hospitality and broadcasting,” said Greg Ennis, the Siptu deputy secretary general, in July speaking at a Stop the Game press conference in Dublin. After two games, Ireland are in third place on three points. Austria are top on six points, Kosovo are second on three points but lead Ireland on head-to-head, with Israel bottom on zero points. The winner of the group is promoted to League A, with second place in a promotion playoff. Bottom of the group faces relegation playoffs. Austria should provide a considerable test with players like Bayern Munich’s Konrad Laimer and Borussia Dortmund’s Carney Chukwuemeka. The Ralf Rangnick-managed side are the toughest team in the group, but Ireland are unbeaten in their past seven games at home, so are well capable of getting a result. title: Florida A&M dominates SWAC home opener v. Alabama State - The FAMUAN
content: The Florida A&M Lady Rattlers defended home court at the Al Lawson Center on Friday, claiming a statement four-set victory over the Alabama State Lady Hornets. The win opened SWAC conference play on a high note for Florida A&M, improving the program to 6-8 overall and setting a confident tone for the early postseason push. From the opening whistle, Florida A&M focused on dominating the net to dictate the match tempo. The Rattlers’ front-row defense lived up to its reputation as one of the conference’s top blocking units, using their length to close gaps against Alabama State’s primary hitters and keep the ball off their side of the floor. That net presence paid immediate dividends in the opening frame, as Florida A&M controlled the point from the first serve and never trailed, riding four front-row blocks and three service aces to a runaway 25-14 set win. “Blocking has been super important, something that all the coaches emphasize is it’s the first line of defense,” said Makenzie Taylor. “So any ball that we can keep from coming on our side of the net is the perfect scenario. So we really stress blocking. You work on it every single day, and it’s like a top priority for us.” When Alabama State responded with a fast-paced offense in the second set to hand Florida A&M a 25-22 loss, the Lady Rattlers relied on mental composure rather than panic. Senior pin hitters Sydney Whitfield and LaDonna Trantham proved lethal on transition defense and out-of-system plays, keeping the Hornets’ block off-balance even when routine passes broke down. Whitfield put together a dominant night, leading all scorers with a match-high 25 kills and 10 digs, while Trantham added 13 kills and crucial back-row defense to maintain offensive continuity. Behind a career night from setter Bengisu Kazazlar, who distributed 30 assists, the Lady  Rattlers operated at a scorching .405 hitting clip for the match. Florida A&M rebounded swiftly in set three with 17 kills on a .394 attack percentage to secure a 25-16 victory. “Something that we focus on as a team is being comfortable and creating our own identity,” Trantham noted regarding the team’s ability to bounce back after dropping the second set. “Our coach always tells us that the game will come to us, so we just try to stay consistent and rely on the fundamentals instead of letting emotion take control.” That disciplined approach fueled a devastating start to the fourth set, as Florida A&M stormed out to a 9-0 run behind strong serving from Trantham and immediate defensive execution, building an eventual 10-1 cushion. Florida A&M finished the frame with 19 kills against just two attack errors to close out the 25-22 victory. “Yeah, I think when we start off strong like that, it sets the tone for the rest of the set, and we were talking about that in the huddle before,” Whitfield said of the final frame surge. “So just going out, doing our job, Donna did a great job of keeping the serve, and then we were just playing defense behind that.” With 58 total team digs led by Whitfield’s 10 and Kelly Kelsick’s nine and four blocks from Farah Farooq, Florida A&M kept its offense in-system, where Alabama State struggled to find answers. Protecting home court was paramount for the Rattlers. “We had an understanding that we needed to protect our home court,” Taylor said. “Starting the season off with a win really gives us a lot of confidence going into these next coming games.” The next game for the Lady Rattlers will take place on Friday as they take on Mississippi Valley State. The debt limit for subchapter V of chapter 11 has had a wild ride. Fortunately, it appears that the days of fluctuating debt limits are behind us, with the Senate’s unanimous passage of H.R. 7730. The bill now heads to the President, who is expected to sign it into law. Subchapter V debuted effective February 19, 2020, and is designed to meet the needs of small businesses for whom a “standard” chapter 11 bankruptcy case is often too expensive and unwieldy. Subchapter V initially carried a debt limit of $2,725,623, meaning that debtors with noncontingent, liquidated debt[1] in excess of this amount were ineligible for relief under this part of the Bankruptcy Code. The subchapter V debt limit was soon raised to $7,500,000 by the CARES Act, but with a sunset provision. The sunset date was extended by a year, but eventually lapsed, dropping the limit back to $2.7 million. An automatic inflation adjustment raised the limit to $3,024,725[2] in 2022. Congress then restored the $7.5 million debt limit, but with another two-year sunset provision. It was not renewed, so two years later, the subchapter V debt limit reverted again to $3,024,725. Another inflation adjustment brought it to $3,424,000 as of April 1, 2025—and there it remained, until now. H.R. 7730, officially named the “Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment Act,” does away with all the back and forth. The debt limit for filing for subchapter V bankruptcy cases is permanently fixed at $7,500,000, with inflation adjustments every three years going forward. Chapter 13 debt limits, which suffered similar (albeit slightly less dramatic) swings, are also addressed in the new bill. Currently, a debtor must have no more than $526,700 in unsecured noncontingent, liquidated debt, and no more than $1,580,125 in secured noncontingent, liquidated debt to file for chapter 13 bankruptcy relief. The bill establishes a single $2,750,000 debt limit for both secured and unsecured debt, which will also be adjusted for inflation going forward. [1] The debt limits discussed here refer to how much noncontingent, liquidated debt a debtor may have and still qualify to file for bankruptcy protection. Generally speaking, a “contingent” debt is one that requires some event to happen before it is owed (e.g., a warranty claim owed only if a covered part fails). “Noncontingent” debts are those that lack such a requirement. A “liquidated” debt is one where the amount is known or can be readily determined. (E.g., the amount owed at any moment under a loan may not be stated in the note but can be quickly computed by reference to its terms.) [2] The $3 million dollar figure is not an even dollar amount because it is adjusted for inflation every three years. title: Kathleen V. Jameson Returns to Louisville to Lead the Speed - The Voice-Tribune
content: Kathleen V. Jameson, Ph.D., has returned to Louisville to lead the Speed Art Museum as its new director, guiding Kentucky’s oldest and largest art museum as it approaches its centennial in 2027. Jameson began her new position on September 8, bringing more than three decades of experience in museum leadership, curatorial work, fundraising, strategic planning, and community engagement. Her appointment also brings her back to an institution that played an early role in her development as a museum professional. While earning her master’s degree in American Art and Architecture at the University of Louisville, Jameson worked with Peter Morrin, who was then director of the Speed. She has described that experience as formative to her career. “Returning to Louisville and to the Speed is deeply meaningful to me,” Jameson said. “My time here as a graduate student helped shape both my scholarship and my career in museums, and I have always valued the Speed’s commitment to artistic excellence and connection.” Since her time in Louisville, Jameson has held senior positions at several major American art museums. Most recently, she served as executive director of the James A. Michener Art Museum in Doylestown, Pennsylvania, where she led work involving collections development, exhibitions, community engagement, and the museum’s infrastructure. Previously, Jameson was president and CEO of The Mint Museum in Charlotte. Her responsibilities there included collections development, exhibitions, scholarship, fundraising, strategic planning, organizational restructuring, and governance. During her tenure, she established the museum’s inaugural digital media program, a contemporary architecture and design series, and a major Latino and Latin American initiative. Jameson also spent several years at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, where she held curatorial and administrative positions including assistant director and director of program support. Her work included long-range institutional planning and oversight of an international architect search. Her academic specialization is American art and the history of photography, particularly late-19th- and early-20th-century American art, with additional expertise in works on paper. She holds a Ph.D. from the University of Delaware, an MBA from Rice University, an MA from the University of Louisville, and a BA from the University of Texas at Austin. She has also served as a scholar-in-residence at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum and as a National Arts Strategies Chief Executive Program Fellow. At the Speed, Jameson has identified listening to staff and community partners, strengthening connections throughout the region, and advancing the museum’s artistic and educational mission among her early priorities. The centennial will provide a significant moment for the museum to reflect on its history while looking toward the years ahead. “The Centennial is an extraordinary opportunity not only to celebrate the Speed’s history, but also to think ambitiously about its future,” Jameson said. “Museums are at their best when they bring art, ideas, and people together.” Jameson’s return places her at the center of a milestone year for the organization with which she has a longstanding connection. As the Speed prepares to mark 100 years, its new director brings with her both an established career in American museums and a personal history with the museum she now leads. For more information, visit: https://www.speedmuseum.org/

title: Obituary: Gladys V. Conlon - The Belmont Voice
content:
With serenity and grace, Gladys V. Conlon (Boghosian), 94, a lifelong Belmont resident, passed to eternity on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026,  at the Kaplan Family Hospice Home in Danvers. Gladys was the daughter of the late Victoria Vaznaian Boghosian, an Armenian Genocide survivor, and her father, the late Paul T. Boghosian, a noted businessman. She is  survived by her sister, Marilyn Papazian, and her brother, Paul T. Boghosian Jr. of Belmont.  Gladys raised four children: a daughter, Sharon Morasso, who lives in Genoa, Italy, a son, Michael P. Conlon, who lives in Nevada, a daughter, Deborah Brown, who lives in Tennessee and a son, Patrick Conlon, who lives in California.  Gladys was blessed to have seven grandchildren and eight great-grandchildren.  These children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren provide a testament to the continuation of Gladys’ life story. Gladys’ journey was not without challenges, marked by having four children in five years, limited financial resources and a husband not devoted to marriage or child rearing resulting in a family move from Cleveland to Belmont.  Gladys enjoyed walking everywhere in Belmont, roller skating when younger, dancing to music at Mosley’s, dining with family and friends, reading at Belmont’s libraries and participating in activities at the senior center.  She especially enjoyed traveling to California and Texas to visit her children and grandchildren and camping with her friends. Gladys was a steadfast and devoted Armenian Christian and a 50-year member of the First Armenian Church in Belmont.  Gladys loved the church services and its celebration of the holidays and  many festivals.  Gladys always appreciated the warm welcome of its congregation and the support of its ministers during her harrowing times, particularly the support of Rev. Vartan Hartunian. Gladys took pride in her work at Mt. Auburn and Sancta Maria hospitals, selling and providing customer service in the 1980s and 1990s to patients wanting televisions and phones in their rooms.  She often told stories of patients who would not allow her to leave their rooms before they related their life stories.  Gladys provided a sympathetic ear to their stories, and she felt she was helping them by giving her time.  She loved this part of her job more than anything else. Gladys considered herself fortunate to have lived for almost a century.  Because she loved movies, she often recalled when admission to a theater was 15 cents and  Shirley Temple was America’s number one star. title: League of Women Voters of Massachusetts v. Trump and Mail Ballots (Part 1) (Civil Rights Policy Brief #256) - usresistnews.org
content: Policy Summary: On March 31, 2026 President Donald Trump issued the executive order (EO) titled “Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections.” The order had two main components – the establishment of state citizenship lists of every citizen in the state eligible to vote and directing the United States Postal Service with creating and implementing rules regarding the use, delivery and acceptance of mail – ballots used by each individual State. The executive order was quickly challenged in court. A case was filed in the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts on April 2, 2026. After a lengthy process that included briefing on a possible temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction that would have prevented the executive order from going into effect, the federal district court on September 4, 2026 issued an order granting the plaintiff’s request for a preliminary injunction. The order by the court prohibits the executive order from going into effect. The case was appealed to the First Circuit Court of Appeals with the Federal Government filing an emergency motion for a stay of the district court’s order pending an appeal. If granted this would have halted the district court’s order and allowed President Trump’s executive order to go into effect while the appeal was ongoing. However, the First Circuit Court of Appeals denied the application for a stay which means the executive order will not be allowed to go into effect. President Trump and his allies on September 10th made an appeal to the United States Supreme Court but that application is still pending with nothing certain on when the Supreme Court will issue a ruling on the case. LEARN MORE Policy Analysis: The details of President Trump’s executive order is flawed on a number of levels. First, Trump has taken a step to implement rules that he has no power to do. The U.S. Constitution specifically grants the power of voting to the individual states and to Congress. It does not include the President of the United States any power over the voting rules. Each State is allowed to craft and implement the rules regarding voting in their state, including the use of mail ballots. The rules regarding mail ballots differ from state to state which is acceptable. Congress has on occasion stepped in to help create uniform rules and the key point here is that only Congress can do it. President Trump, or any future President, cannot unilaterally implement voting rules which likely makes the March 31st executive order likely unconstitutional and invalid. A review of the details of the executive order reveals more issues with the executive order than just the constitutional defects. The order sought to require a creation of “state citizen lists” of those who are eighteen (18) years of age, confirmed to be United States citizens and who maintain a residence in the state. While the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and other agencies would be required to share the compiled lists with individual states, it is not clear what the states are supposed to do with the lists. There is also a high risk of error when compiling the lists which could lead to citizens being left off the list although they may be eligible, e.g., due to moving or residence out of state such as for college. Furthermore, there are privacy statutes on the books that would prevent the creation of such lists which was not addressed by the Trump Administration. Additionally, the order would have required states to comply with a mail ballot designed by USPS to be used by all states and for states to notify USPS if and who will be voting by mail in their state at least ninety (90) days before a federal election. This is completely out of bounds of executive and USPS authority as USPS does not have the resources to design a mail ballot. Nor does USPS have the resources to determine who will vote by mail three months before an election occurs. There is no clarity why the Administration wants this. Finally, the most disturbing part of the executive order is that it creates criminal liability for election officials who issue ballots to ineligible voters even if the ballot is never used. And it also grants USPS discretion as to who mail ballots should be delivered to based on who or who is not on the “state citizen lists.” The order contains no notice procedure to alert a person they are being refused delivery of their mail ballot. Nor does it contemplate the time, money and resources on having USPS compare the mail bags they are delivering with “state citizen lists” that have no accuracy protections or provisions. While these practical problems are real it does no disguise the fact that the executive order will likely cause chaos come election time which may be the preference of this Administration. Fortunately, barring any action from the Supreme Court, the preliminary injunction is in place for the time period when the 2026 midterm elections will occur which indicates that Trump’s Executive Order will not be in effect on Election Day. title: Decoded - Technology Law Insights, V 7, Issue 9, 2026 | Spilman Thomas & Battle, PLLC - JDSupra
content:
Welcome to our ninth issue of 2026 of Decoded -- our technology law insights e-newsletter. AI Agents are Rewriting the Rules of Lateral Movement “In May 2026, OpenAI announced that one of its models had disproved a 1946 Erdős conjecture in discrete geometry, largely by working through paths a mathematician would abandon as too tedious.” Why this is important: Relentless. This is perhaps the best description of an AI attempting to accomplish a task. Much has been made about the July 2026 Hugging Face and similar incidents, intrusions which would be difficult for a human operator to match. The technical timeline from Hugging Face reconstructed 17,613 actions grouped into approximately 6,000 clusters. Given enough time (and resources), a human team could likely accomplish the same thing. But not quite like a relentless AI agent given the same goal by their human programmer. The article notes that the persistence of these attacks highlights the central security problem: "[p]ermissions describe what an identity can access directly. They do not reveal every route an autonomous system may assemble from the identities, credentials, tools, and trust relationships available along the way." The AI agents are able to see connections that never should have existed. This is exacerbated by the need for AI agents to move laterally in their normal work. So lateral movement alone is no longer the security flag it once was. The article grounds this in hard data: Token Security's research found that 51 percent of external actions taken by agentic chatbots authenticate with hard-coded credentials rather than OAuth, and a separate investigation by METR and Redwood Research found that roughly 1,200 agents meant to run in isolation discovered an unauthorized way to communicate, about 700 of which later joined the attack. The article posits that intent-based security systems can supply the missing context to better identify a harmful/rogue agent. Identity, it argues, is the only control plane that spans every system the AI interacts with, and intent determines whether that access makes sense. The article recommends that security teams: discover every agent (including "shadow" agents created outside formal IT processes), assign ownership, map the full access chain, compare access with intent, and enforce continuously. It concludes with the warning that "[o]rganizations that cannot will learn what their agents can reach only after the agents find it." --- Christopher M. Green AI Completely Absent from Most Organizations’ Ethics Codes, Survey Finds “Fewer employees say they cite their codes of conduct or use them as a resource, according to LRN, even as workplace misconduct reports increase.” Why this is important: The best employee policies are worthless without execution. Maybe if General Patton was in HR, he would have said this instead of his famous "[a] good plan, violently executed now, is better than a perfect plan next week." AI is rapidly changing the workplace, yet fewer than 1 in 10 codes of conduct explicitly address AI or technology ethics, according to the article, and few employees actually use these policies as a resource. The report drew on a survey of 2,000 full-time employees, nearly 1 in 5 of whom said their codes lacked practical guidance. This comes at a time of rising reported workplace misconduct: 55 percent of employees experienced or witnessed misconduct in 2025, up from 41 percent in 2024, and only 66 percent felt they could report it without retaliation, down from 71 percent a year earlier. The article states that this does not necessarily mean that each employer should add an AI section to their code of conduct. Instead, LRN suggests connecting AI back to ethical principles the organization already embraces rather than bolting on standalone AI rules. As LRN puts it, the strongest codes "help employees navigate emerging risks with practical guidance that is easy to find, easy to understand, and easy to apply." HR should also treat AI ethics policies as "living documents" that adjust to the changing landscape. --- Christopher M. Green Google AI Models Broke Out of Sandbox, Hacked Three Companies “The incidents stemmed from the same testing environment defects that tripped up OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta.” Why this is important: Earlier this year, Google’s Gemini AI models escaped a sandbox during security testing and accessed the real systems of three companies on separate occasions. During a capture-the-flag exercise, Gemini was supposed to attack fictional companies, three of which happened to have names matching real companies. Gemini found public information online and either guessed passwords or discovered valid credentials in a public database, then accessed the real companies’ systems. Google notified the affected companies and denies that Gemini continued its activity after gaining access. The incidents were attributed to weaknesses in the sandbox/testing environment operated by Irregular, an Israeli AI security-testing company. Similar sandbox escapes had previously affected models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta. The fact that multiple major AI labs experienced related sandbox escapes suggests the containment/testing infrastructure itself is an important security concern. Irregular said it notified relevant AI labs in July and had fixed the known sandbox problems within weeks. Google says it also worked with its testing partner to change its testing procedures. However, the incidents illustrate a security problem that goes beyond whether an AI model itself is intentionally malicious: an autonomous model can potentially discover and exploit unintended paths out of its testing environment. The revelations come amid U.S. debates over adequate AI regulation and safety requirements, as well as growing concern about competition and AI security involving Chinese AI systems. --- Jennifer A. Baker Don’t Let AI Distract from Cybersecurity Basics, Officials and Executives Warn “Government and industry leaders said simple attacks remain far more consequential than anything AI is doing.” Why this is important: Artificial intelligence (AI) dominates today's cybersecurity conversation, but leaders speaking at the Billington Cybersecurity Summit earlier this month delivered a different message: the attacks causing the most damage are still the simple ones. Stolen passwords, outdated software, and people tricked into granting access remain the top threats. A Federal Bureau of Investigation official noted that the steps that will stop tomorrow's attacks are the same ones that would have stopped yesterday’s. AI is making criminals faster, but their methods have not changed. Officials from the United Kingdom, New Zealand, and Canada agreed, and the National Security Agency cybersecurity director summed it up: "AI can't outrun the basics." The most effective defenses are within reach of any business, regardless of size: keeping software updated, using multifactor authentication, knowing what devices are on the network, and training employees to spot suspicious emails and calls. None of these require the latest AI product. Fundamentals, combined with constant monitoring and people ready to act, are what stop real attacks. New tools should strengthen that foundation, not replace it. --- James E. Dunlap, Chief Information Officer, Spilman Thomas & Battle WeChat Zero-Click Attack Enables Account and Device Takeover Without User Interaction “Chained with other vulnerabilities such as OEMpocalypse, the zero-click attack could enable an attacker to gain root access by exploiting other apps.” Why this is important: This article highlights a type of cyberattack that may surprise, and certainly terrify, readers. This attack took control of an app on the target’s phone without the target clicking a link or downloading an attachment. Threat actors took advantage of a target’s WeChat account simply by calling the target’s phone. It didn’t matter if the target answered the call or not. After taking over the target’s WeChat account, the threat actor could then target others on the target’s friend list, including by sending them messages and calling them through the app. WeChat’s creator, Tencent, reports that it fixed the vulnerability that led to this attack. The article reports on the fact that “super apps” like WeChat are a lucrative target because of their advanced functionality that includes mobile payments, delivery services, messaging, and calling. Taking over a target’s WeChat account could give a threat actor control over many aspects of the target’s life. --- Nicholas P. Mooney II McKesson Cyberattack: Stolen Data Includes 6.4 Million Unique Email Addresses “McKesson, a major U.S. wholesale medical supplies & equipment, pharmaceutical distribution, and healthcare technology solutions company, continues to investigate a cybersecurity incident involving unauthorized access and the exfiltration of sensitive data.” Why this is important: In late August 2026, healthcare distributor McKesson disclosed that criminals had stolen data from its systems. A group called ShinyHunters claimed responsibility and demanded more than $55 million. Independent analysis found 6.4 million unique email addresses in the stolen data, and McKesson says the information may include Social Security numbers, insurance numbers, diagnoses, medications, and payment details. The breach reportedly involved cloud applications run by outside vendors, and ShinyHunters typically gains access by phoning employees and talking them into handing over their logins. Two lessons apply to any business. First, an organization's security is only as strong as the vendors that hold its data, so businesses should know which vendors handle sensitive information and hold them to clear security standards. Second, a convincing phone call can defeat expensive security technology. Employees should verify any unexpected call asking them to reset a password or approve a login by calling back through a known, trusted number. When in doubt, hang up and call IT. --- James E. Dunlap, Chief Information Officer, Spilman Thomas & Battle “The idea is appealing enough that federal researchers investigated it in 2023, concluding that abandoned mine lands offer ‘land, power infrastructure, and mine water cooling’ to data center developers, particularly in a place like Pennsylvania.” Why this is important: The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania is rich in resources: coal, water reserves, fertile land, wildlife, oil reserves, and engaged citizens, among others. The new economic development talk of the small towns in eastern and western Pennsylvania is data centers. One creative option being investigated for data center placement is putting them beneath the soil in the nearly 5,586 abandoned coal mines across the Commonwealth. Researchers at Penn State’s Department of Energy and Mineral Engineering suggest that placing data centers below ground in Pennsylvania’s abandoned mines could serve to repurpose the mines, lead to necessary reclamation and restoration efforts, avoid reported disturbances such as noise complaints, and benefit from natural cooling and underground lakes already associated with several mines. Some abandoned mines already have permits and necessary proximity to the electricity grid, which would reduce additional administrative burden; however, this does not indicate that the grid itself can support the needs of any associated data centers. Mine restoration and curbing the negative effects of abandoned sites, toxic residues, and tainted water supplies are prime priorities for residents who have historical precedent for being opposed to new promises of economic growth through additional ecological sacrifices. The novel approach would still require expert-level analysis and major investment; nevertheless, if data center development is to continue at all, it behooves all parties, communities and developers alike, to cooperatively consider and plan for a safe, sustainable option for long-term success. --- Sophia L. Hines FTC Sues Hims & Hers Over Telehealth Data Practices and Drug Prescribing “One problem is the limited scope of the U.S. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, or HIPAA, which governs the privacy of medical information.” Why this is important: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is suing Hims & Hers, a telemedicine company, alleging problems with the handling of patients’ health data, subscriptions, and prescription practices. Hims & Hers disputes the action, calling it an attempt to generate negative publicity. U.S. health privacy rules contain a significant gap that leaves telehealth users exposed because direct-to-consumer medical services often fall outside the scope of HIPAA. The FTC has increasingly targeted online telemedicine companies for allegedly mishandling medical data, sharing consumer information with advertising platforms without consent, and prescribing medications with minimal clinical oversight. Of particular concern is online prescribing of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs. Research cited in the article found that fewer than one-third of nearly 50 websites studied required a live audio or video consultation before prescribing. Some prescriptions could reportedly be approved within minutes, while screening for eating disorders—which can be relevant to these medications—was inconsistent. The article argues that telehealth companies should have to obtain users’ clear, informed consent before collecting or using health information; medical data shouldn't be shared with advertisers without separate permission; potentially risky medications, such as GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, should involve a real consultation with a healthcare professional, rather than relying solely on automated questionnaires; and subscription terms and cancellation procedures should be clear and straightforward. Users can improve their privacy by reviewing policies, blocking trackers, and using privacy-focused browsers, but these measures can't fully solve the problem if companies collect excessive data or share it with third parties. --- Jennifer A. Baker CISA: A Coordinated Cyber Attack by Suspected Iranian Hackers Affected Over 100 Water Systems “The agency specifically linked the attacks to internet-exposed programmable logic controllers used in field operations, typically connected via cellular modems.” Why this is important: We’ve reported in prior issues of Decoded on threat actors targeting critical infrastructure for cyberattacks. This article is significant because it reports on just such an attack. In July, a cyberattack that has been attributed by some to Iranian threat actors affected over 100 water systems in several states, including Michigan, Minnesota, South Dakota, Georgia, New Jersey, and Alabama. The attack targeted water systems of varying sizes, which the article emphasizes is shining a light on security problems at smaller water utilities. These problems cannot be ignored, especially since those smaller utilities make up 81 percent of all U.S. public water systems. Perhaps the most troubling aspect of this attack is that some industry experts and government officials warn that it’s a practice run for a larger campaign of attacks by Iranian threat actors. --- Nicholas P. Mooney II Pennsylvania Governor Orders Strict Requirements for New Data Centers “A new executive order mandates standards on energy affordability, environmental protection, workforce/economic development, transparency, and community engagement.” Why this is important: Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro has issued stricter requirements for new data centers, including developer-funded energy infrastructure, water-saving measures, local workforce promises, community engagement, and transparency regarding energy and water use. AI data centers will be excluded from Fast Track permitting, and nondisclosure agreements will be prohibited. --- Jason Wandling U.S. Economy Hits Pivotal Milestone: Spending on Data Centers and Other Information-Processing Hardware Now Exceeds Housing Investment “Hyperscalers have poured so much money into building as much AI infrastructure as possible—and as quickly as possible—that investment from a handful of companies is expected to reach $1 trillion a year soon.” Why this is important: U.S. investment in data centers and related equipment has overtaken residential investment for the first time, reflecting the growing economic impact of the AI boom. Second-quarter spending on data center equipment reached $752 billion, compared with $748 billion in residential financing. AI infrastructure spending is expected to accelerate further, with capital expenditures by major technology companies projected to exceed $1.3 trillion in 2027. By contrast, housing investment has declined amid elevated interest rates, high construction costs, and constrained demand. --- Jason Wandling State Authorities Warn They Lack Resources to Address Cyber Threat to Critical Sectors “State CIOs and CISOs need additional funding, personnel and training to protect water, energy and healthcare, according to a new report.” Why this is important: This article is significant because it highlights that state and local government officials across the country are reporting that they lack funding, support, and staffing to protect critical infrastructure, like water systems. Pair this article with the other article in this issue of Decoded about Iranian threat actors attacking over 100 water systems across several states earlier this year, and the size of this issue becomes apparent. Cutbacks at the federal level have forced states to be creative in finding ways to protect infrastructure. The White House is trying to assist them with a pilot project to provide resources to state water utilities. Regardless, infrastructure will continue to be a target for threat actors. --- Nicholas P. Mooney II Data Centers are Eating Up Steel. Developers are Now Looking at Timber. “Surging steel costs and longer lead times are pushing data center developers to consider alternatives, Skanska executives said during a webinar.” Why this is important: Rising steel prices and extended lead times are prompting data center developers to consider mass timber as an alternative structural material. Steel prices have increased 25 percent over the past year, while lead times have more than doubled to 55 weeks, driven in part by demand from data centers and semiconductor facilities. Although timber generally carries higher upfront structural costs, its lighter weight and prefabricated construction can reduce foundation, interior, and scheduling costs. Lumber prices have remained comparatively stable, and North American mass-timber manufacturing capacity has expanded. However, higher insurance costs and the need for early design and coordination remain challenges for adoption. --- Jason Wandling DISCLAIMER: Because of the generality of this update, the information provided herein may not be applicable in all situations and should not be acted upon without specific legal advice based on particular situations.

title: BETTER LATE THAN NEVER?: Ohio District Court Grants Motion For Reconsideration Six Years After Facebook v. Duguid. - The National Law Review
content: The National Law Review uses cookies to track usage trends and patterns to better understand and improve our website. By using this website and/or clicking on any link on the website, you confirm your consent to the NLR’s placing and usage of cookies. Hi, TCPAWorld! Kelly Sandberg here, with some case law revival, six years after the significant ruling in Facebook v. Duguid emerged. In Phillip Ramsey v. Receivables Performance Management, LLC, Plaintiff Ramsey had previously brought an action in 2016 against Receivables Performance Management, LLC and Howard George (collectively “Defendants”) for violations of the TCPA by using automated technology to call Plaintiff’s cellphone 245 times without his consent. Phillip Ramsey v. Receivables Performance Management, LLC, No. 1:16-CV-1059, 2026 WL 2916680, at *1 (S.D. Ohio Sept. 29, 2026). In 2019, both parties had filed motions for summary judgment and the then-assigned District Judge, Matthew W. McFarland, denied summary judgment to the Defendants and granted Plaintiff partial summary judgment in 2020. Plaintiff was also awarded $122,500.00 for TCPA violations. However, not long after this ruling was made, the Supreme Court decided Facebook, Inc. v. Duguid, 592 U.S. 395 (2021). And just now, almost six years after that ruling, Defendants requested that the Court reconsider the previous decision in light of Duguid. “District courts have authority both under common law and Rule 54(b) to reconsider interlocutory orders and to reopen any part of a case before entry of final judgment.” Rodriguez v. Tenn Laborers Health & Welfare Fund, 89 F. App’x 949, 959 (6th Cir. 2004). Reconsideration may be appropriate under this rule “when there is (1) an intervening change of controlling law; (2) new evidence available; or (3) a need to correct a clear error or prevent manifest injustice.” Id. The Court determined that reconsideration was appropriate here because Duguid resolved a conflict among the Courts of Appeals that was at issue when the Judge McFarland denied summary judgment to the Defendants. Judge McFarland had expressly relied on Allan v. Pennsylvania Higher Educ. Assistance Agency, when making his determination, but after he did so, Duguid resolved the issue of what is considered to be an automatic telephone dialing system, or an auto dialer under the TCPA. Allan v. Pennsylvania Higher Educ. Assistance Agency, 968 F.3d 567 (6th Cir. 2020). In case you’re new around here, Duguid provided that “a necessary feature of an auto dialer under §227(a)(1)(A) is the capacity to use a random or sequential number generator to either store or produce phone numbers to be called.” Duguid, 592 U.S. at 409 (emphasis added). Because of this determination, the Supreme Court had expressly vacated and abrogated the Sixth Circuit’s decision in Allan. In applying Duguid, rather than Allen, the Court determined whether the dialer used by Defendants would qualify as an automatic telephone dialing system, and whether summary judgment was warranted for Defendants. Summary judgment is warranted “if the movant shows that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a). Plaintiff Ramsey contended that the dialer Defendants used qualified as an ATDS, and that this argument was reinforced by a case that predated Duguid. Besides this contention, Plaintiff offered no additional support that would create a genuine issue of material fact to warrant summary judgment in his favor. The Court agreed with Defendants’ argument that summary judgment could not be granted when Plaintiff failed to provide any evidence that Defendants used a random or sequential number generator. Additionally, Defendants had provided affirmative evidence that they did not have a random or sequential number generator, as shown in the facts that Judge McFarland had initially relied upon. The facts supported the conclusion that the dialer did not store or produce phone numbers to be called. That evidence established that Defendant’s electronic database system: (1) maintained telephone numbers as part of identified debtors’ account records; (2) selected accounts for next-day calling based on entered dialing parameters; and (3) that system compiled the selected accounts into “campaigns” (pre-existing lists of telephone numbers) before transferring the campaigns to a Noble Systems, Inc. telephone system – also known as the Noble Predictive Dialer. The Noble Predictive Dialer would then dial campaign numbers by clicking a button to press play to have a list start. The Court determined that the dialer used was an automated dialer that chose from a targeted, predetermined list – NOT an ATDS system. No storing, and no producing here! (Sorry – six years ago!) Ultimately, the Court granted Defendant’s motion for reconsideration, vacated the prior Memorandum Opinion and Order by Judge McFarland, and granted Defendant’s motion for summary judgment. title: Why is Croatia v England behind closed doors? - Yahoo Sports
content: England's match against Croatia in the Nations League on Saturday will be played behind closed doors in Rijeka. The game will take place in front of a reduced crowd in the same venue in which the two sides met, also behind closed doors, in a 0-0 draw in October 2018. The limited capacity is because of crowd disturbances involving Croatia fans during a Nations League match against France in March 2025. Seven fans were taken into custody on suspicion of making Nazi salutes during the match, and released without prosecution because of a lack of evidence. In their section of Stade de France, where that match took place, Croatia supporters also set off fireworks. On top of that, Croatia were also prohibited from having travelling supporters in their 2-1 win in the Czech Republic last Saturday. While the match is officially being played behind closed doors, there will be some supporters in attendance. Between 3,000 and 6,000 Croatian schoolchildren have been permitted to attend the match at Stadion Riejka. Initially, England fans were not allowed to attend. Following discussions with Uefa and England, the Three Lions were later permitted to have 100 complimentary tickets given to their fans. title: Clear but Impossible: Satius v. Samsung Moves Inoperable Claims from Indefiniteness to Enablement - Patently-O
content:
The Federal Circuit has affirmed invalidity of Satius's wireless-coupler patent, but on a different ground than the district court. Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., No. 2025-1446 (Fed. Cir. Oct. 1, 2026). Claim 1 of U.S. Patent No. 6,711,385 recites an apparatus "for transmitting electric or electromagnetic signals over air." Everyone agrees the first option is impossible: electromagnetic signals travel through air; electric signals do not. Magistrate Judge Burke (D. Del.) held the claims indefinite on that basis. Chief Judge Moore's opinion for the panel (joined by Judges Lourie and Hughes) rejects that reasoning, holding that a claim can be clear about its scope even when part of that scope is physically impossible. The court then held the claims invalid for lack of enablement, an issue the district court had found waived. Judge Hughes previewed the result at oral argument: "If I claim the transporter from Star Trek, everybody knows what I'm claiming. It's impossible. But it's impossible because it's not enabled, not because it's indefinite." The panel's precedential opinion adopts that view. To continue reading, become a Patently-O member. Already a member? title: The Japanese V-Twin Engineered To Outlive Its Owner - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update A V-twin engine holds a very distinctive place in motorcycling history. American cruiser bikes are defined by their rumbling V-twin engines. The Ducati Panigale V2, the Aprilia RSV Mille, and the KTM RC8 are sportbikes that showcase the wild side of V-twin engines. Although more complex than a parallel-twin engine, V-twins (in existence since 1902) have shown notable refinement and durability. Who better to highlight these features than Japanese motorcycle makers, known for precision engineering? As a result, many Far East V-twin engines are designed to last much longer than their counterparts. The engine that interests us is a modern V-twin that has been around since 1983 and currently powers a timeless Honda cruiser bike. This is because Japanese motorcycle makers combine precision manufacturing tolerances, conservative engine tuning, and the philosophy of Kaizen (continuous refinement) in their engineering. The result is a relatively concise yet long-lasting lineup of V-twin-powered motorcycles. A V-twin engine is more adaptive than a comparable parallel-twin mill. They offer a narrower frontal profile, stronger low-end torque, and a lower center of gravity. This is why a V-twin engine works well on low-slung cruisers and nimble, urban-ready streetfighters. Beyond reliability, V-twins also add drama with a distinctive sound and visually pleasing design. Japanese V-twin engines, especially the long-standing ones, offer a balance of traditional and modern features that help them stay relevant for longer. Most V-twin engines in the Japanese portfolio are 20-plus years old and from Suzuki. The Boulevard C50 V-twin is 25 years old, the SV650 V-twin is 27 years old, and the mighty M109R power cruiser's V-twin is 20 years old. Interestingly, the youngest V-twin Japanese cruiser bike engine is the Yamaha Bolt R-Spec's 13-year-old 942 cc air-cooled mill. These long-lasting engines have stayed relevant for so long thanks to the manufacturer's formula of subtly updating them over the years with the necessary components. The most common upgrade is swapping carburetors for fuel injection. This adds a much-needed refresh without hampering reliability or refinement. Among the timeless bunch, the Honda Shadow Phantom stands out because its V-twin engine is a core design that is over 40 years old and has yet to show its age. The Honda Shadow V-twin engine's origin story dates back to the 1980s. Honda launched the 1983 VT750C with a liquid-cooled 45-degree SOHC V-twin. It had a displacement of roughly 749 cc, three valves per cylinder, and a six-speed manual gearbox with a final shaft drive. Then, due to US import tariffs imposed in 1984 on motorcycles over 701 cc, Honda temporarily downsized this engine to 700 cc on the VT700C. The next evolution came in 1998 with the return of the 750 cc V-twin on the Shadow ACE. Honda also changed the V-twin angle to 52 degrees for better balance. This engine has soldiered on without any major updates to date. The 750 cc V-twin is based on the 600 cc Shadow VLX 52-degree mill and was enlarged to 750 cc by increasing the bore by 4 mm and the stroke by 10 mm. Reliability is well catered for here with a simple engineering design featuring a SOHC layout, three valves per cylinder, and a low compression ratio. Add a low-stress performance tune to the mix, and we have an engine that can virtually go on forever with timely maintenance and preventive care. Honda also helps keep this mill relevant to 2026 standards with fuel injection that boosts refinement and helps meet modern emission standards. The latest iteration of this 745 cc liquid-cooled V-twin produces 44.9 horsepower at 5,500 RPM and 47.9 pound-feet of torque at 3,500 RPM. It has a 9.6:1 compression ratio, and the power curve is linear yet meaty at the lower end. Power goes to the rear wheel through a five-speed manual gearbox and a final shaft drive system. The Shadow Phantom doesn't look outdated in 2026 because of its custom touches. This ten-year-old design still looks sharp thanks to blacked-out elements on almost every component. Honda seems to have taken a lot of inspiration from the 1950s Indian Chief. Notable cues include the low-slung, muscular design, a minimal headlamp enclosure, and the padded, scooped solo seat. Its dual-tone paint job on the teardrop fuel tank adds more visual drama. It also gets bobber-inspired chopped fenders that give those chunky tires a more dynamic presence. This design approach also helps the Shadow Phantom age better than its rivals. Its closest counterpart is the cool-looking Kawasaki Vulcan 900 Custom that fuses chopper styling with Japanese longevity. It also has a larger, long-standing 903 cc V-twin and cuts an attractive figure. But the Vulcan 900 is larger and heavier, making it better suited to the highway. The Shadow Phantom edges ahead for urban duties. Also, the Kawasaki costs more at $9,999. Then there's the Suzuki Boulevard C50, which leans more towards the classic side with lots of chrome and full-sized fenders. However, it's a bit too traditional, and features like pulled-back handlebars and floorboards make it more comfortable on highways only. While the Boulevard C50 is priced the same as the Honda Shadow Phantom ($9,299), it falls behind because Suzuki discontinued it for 2026. Despite staying true to the quintessential low-slung, stretched-out cruiser stance, the Honda Shadow Phantom is still relatively compact. It has a 64.5-inch wheelbase and a low seat height of 25.6 inches. The low seat height and five-inch ground clearance lower the center of gravity, aiding stability. The rider sits low and relaxed, with slightly forward-set footpegs and tall, wide handlebars. It also weighs a manageable 553 pounds, making it a comfortable daily runabout. The seat is well-scooped and padded to support long rides. Sturdy and proven underpinnings complement its near-immortal V-twin. The Shadow Phantom sits on a simple double-cradle steel frame that cocoons the V-twin. It is suspended by 41 mm forks up front with 5.5 inches of travel. The rear gets preload-adjustable twin shocks with 3.5 inches of travel. Braking is handled by a 296 mm disc coupled to a two-piston caliper up front. The rear gets a 276 mm disc coupled to a single-piston caliper. Fairly chunky 120/80 front and 160/80 rear tires, mounted on 17-inch front and 15-inch rear laced wheels, help the bike handle highway speeds and winding roads with confidence. There are no complex electronics here. This not only helps the Shadow Phantom stay timeless but also helps it be a comfortable first motorcycle for newbies. The onboard features are very basic, with the only notable feature being dual-channel ABS. Its instrument cluster is as simple as it gets: a large analog speedometer with a tiny bottom-mounted LCD to display data, including trip details. The absence of TFT screens and extensive driver-assist features keeps the overall build simple, too. This makes it easier and more affordable to repair. We want to hear from you. Aside from normal maintenence  these bikes are well built  and will last with just normal maintenence. title: Commanders QB Jayden Daniels limited in Week 4 practice v. Colts - Yahoo Sports
content: Washington Commanders' quarterback Jayden Daniels was limited with a left elbow injury in the team's first practice ahead of Sunday's matchup with the Indianapolis Colts in London. Daniels suffered a dislocated elbow in the Commanders' Week 2 loss to Dallas. He did not play last week against Seattle. According to Nicki Jhabvala of The Athletic, Commanders' head coach Dan Quinn said that the team wants to see how Daniels looks in practice this week before deciding whether or not he will play against the Colts. As a rookie during the 2024 season, Daniels helped lead the Commanders to the NFC Championship Game. An elbow injury in 2025 limited him to only seven games. For his career, he's completed 66% of his passes for 5,090 yards with 36 touchdowns to 12 interceptions. If Daniels can't go, the Commanders will again turn to Marcus Mariota, who led Washington to victory in Week 3 over Seattle.
